reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Most salivary gland tumours occur in the parotid gland and the majority of these are benign, whereas tumours of the smaller submandibular, sublingual, and minor salivary glands carry a proportionally higher risk of malignancy
The typical presentation is a slow-growing, painless lump, and pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign tumour while mucoepidermoid and adenoid cystic carcinomas are common malignant types
Features suggesting malignancy include rapid growth, pain, fixation to surrounding tissue, skin involvement, cervical lymphadenopathy, and especially facial nerve weakness in parotid lesions
Facial nerve palsy in association with a parotid mass is a strong indicator of malignant invasion and demands urgent evaluation
Fine-needle aspiration cytology and imaging help characterise the lesion, though definitive diagnosis often rests on excisional histology
Adenoid cystic carcinoma is notable for perineural spread and a tendency to late recurrence and distant metastasis, requiring prolonged follow-up
Surgery is the primary treatment, with parotidectomy performed to preserve the facial nerve whenever oncologically feasible, and appropriate gland excision for other sites

Radiotherapy is used adjuvantly for high-grade tumours, positive margins, perineural invasion, or nodal disease, while enucleation of pleomorphic adenoma is avoided due to recurrence and malignant transformation risk
reference.pathophysiology: Salivary gland tumours arise from the epithelial and myoepithelial cells of the major and minor salivary glands and comprise a diverse group with widely varying behaviour. Benign tumours such as pleomorphic adenoma grow slowly and are well circumscribed but can recur if incompletely excised and, rarely, undergo malignant transformation over time. Malignant tumours vary from low-grade to aggressive high-grade carcinomas that invade locally, track along nerves (notably adenoid cystic carcinoma), and metastasise to regional nodes and distant sites. The inverse relationship between gland size and malignancy risk reflects the differing tumour types that predominate in each gland.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive or infective lymphadenopathy near the gland
Sialadenitis or salivary duct stones with gland swelling
Metastatic disease to intraparotid lymph nodes
Benign lymphoepithelial lesions and autoimmune sialadenitis
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound as first-line imaging, often with guided fine-needle aspiration cytology
MRI or CT to define tumour extent, deep lobe involvement, and perineural or nodal spread
Assessment of facial nerve function in parotid lesions
Histopathological examination of the excised specimen for type, grade, and margins
Staging imaging for high-grade or clinically malignant tumours
redFlags: Facial nerve weakness accompanying a parotid mass
A rapidly enlarging, painful, or fixed salivary gland lump
Skin ulceration or infiltration over the gland
Associated cervical lymphadenopathy suggesting nodal metastasis
reference.prognosis: Benign tumours have an excellent prognosis after complete excision; malignant tumour outcomes depend on grade, stage, and histological type, with high-grade and adenoid cystic carcinomas prone to recurrence and late distant spread despite treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming all salivary lumps are benign and missing malignant features such as pain or nerve palsy
Enucleating a pleomorphic adenoma, risking recurrence and later malignant transformation
Underestimating perineural spread and late recurrence of adenoid cystic carcinoma
Inadequate facial nerve assessment and counselling before parotid surgery
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Complete surgical excision as the mainstay, with superficial or total parotidectomy and meticulous facial nerve preservation, or excision of the affected submandibular or minor gland
Adequate resection of pleomorphic adenoma with a cuff of normal tissue to prevent recurrence and later malignant transformation
Neck dissection for clinically involved nodes or high-grade malignancy, with sacrifice of infiltrated facial nerve where invaded
Adjuvant radiotherapy for high-grade tumours, positive margins, or adenoid cystic carcinoma with perineural spread
Facial nerve rehabilitation, including grafting or reanimation, where the nerve is sacrificed
Prolonged follow-up, especially for adenoid cystic carcinoma given its tendency to late recurrence and distant metastasis
Management through a head and neck multidisciplinary team integrating surgery, oncology and pathology
